---
title: "Calibrating p-values"
subtitle: "Options, batches and diagnostics"
---

The theory is on the [p-value calibration](../methods/p-values.qmd) page; this
one is about using it.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]

null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
null
```

## One-sided and two-sided

```{python}
args = (null, positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)
print("two-sided:      ", ec.calibrateP(*args)[0])
print("one-sided upper:", ec.calibrateP(*args, twoSided=False, upper=True)[0])
print("one-sided lower:", ec.calibrateP(*args, twoSided=False, upper=False)[0])
```

`upper` is only consulted when `twoSided=False`. Use the upper one-sided test
for safety questions ("does this increase risk?") — it is what MaxSPRT uses.

## Calibrating many estimates at once

`calibrateP` is vectorised; pass whole columns.

```{python}
results = sccs.copy()
results["p_traditional"] = ec.computeTraditionalP(results.logRr, results.seLogRr)
results["p_calibrated"] = ec.calibrateP(null, results.logRr, results.seLogRr)
results.head(8).round(4)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not calibrate a control against a null fitted on itself

The table above includes the negative controls that were used to fit `null`,
which is fine for illustration but is not a valid assessment of those controls.
For that you need leave-one-out — every control calibrated against a null fitted
on the others:

```{python}
neg = negatives.reset_index(drop=True)
loo = [
    ec.calibrateP(
        ec.fitNull(neg.drop(index=i).logRr, neg.drop(index=i).seLogRr),
        neg.logRr[i], neg.seLogRr[i],
    )[0]
    for i in range(len(neg))
]
print(f"{np.mean(np.asarray(loo) < 0.05):.0%} of held-out negative controls "
      f"below 0.05 (nominal 5%)")
```
:::

## Handling missing and infinite values

`calibrateP` returns `nan` for any estimate with a missing or infinite `logRr`
or `seLogRr`, rather than raising:

```{python}
ec.calibrateP(null, [0.2, np.nan, 0.5, np.inf], [0.1, 0.1, np.nan, 0.1])
```

`fitNull` is stricter — it *drops* such estimates before fitting, and warns each
time, because a single infinite value would otherwise dominate the likelihood.
It also drops any estimate with $\lvert\log \mathrm{RR}\rvert > \log 100$, which
in practice means a model that failed to converge.

```{python}
#| warning: true
import warnings

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    ec.fitNull([0.2, np.inf, 0.4], [0.1, 0.1, 0.1])
    for w in caught:
        print(w.message)
```

## Credible intervals via MCMC

When the control set is small, report the uncertainty in the null itself:

```{python}
ec.set_seed(123)
mcmc_null = ec.fitMcmcNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr, iter=10_000)
ec.calibrateP(mcmc_null, positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)
```

Add `pValueOnly=True` to get just the medians as an array, so the call is
drop-in compatible with the point-estimate version.

```{python}
ec.calibrateP(mcmc_null, positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr, pValueOnly=True)
```

## Diagnostics

**Are the controls consistent with the fitted null?** `plotCalibration` shows
the observed distribution of calibrated p-values against uniform.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of negative controls with p below alpha, for every alpha. The solid line is calibrated ('Empirical'), the dash-dot line uncalibrated ('Theoretical'); the faint diagonal is the uniform ideal."
fig = ec.plotCalibration(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
```

**How bad is the uncalibrated test?** `plotExpectedType1Error` turns the fitted
null into the realised type I error rate as a function of precision.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Expected type 1 error under the empirical null. The dashed line is the nominal 5%."
fig = ec.plotExpectedType1Error(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
                                seLogRrPositives=positive.seLogRr, alpha=0.05)
```

**Where does the estimate of interest sit?** `plotCalibrationEffect` places it
against the null band.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Controls, the estimate of interest, and the region where a result would not be significant after calibration."
fig = ec.plotCalibrationEffect(
    negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
    positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr,
    showExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError=True,
)
```

## A reporting pattern

Report both numbers and the null that separates them. The calibrated p-value
alone hides the reason it differs.

```{python}
def calibrated_report(null, logRr, seLogRr, name):
    model = ec.convertNullToErrorModel(null)
    ci = ec.calibrateConfidenceInterval(logRr, seLogRr, model)
    trad = ec.computeTraditionalCi(logRr, seLogRr)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "outcome": [name],
        "rr": [round(float(trad.rr.iloc[0]), 2)],
        "ci": [f"{trad.lb.iloc[0]:.2f}-{trad.ub.iloc[0]:.2f}"],
        "p": [round(float(np.atleast_1d(ec.computeTraditionalP(logRr, seLogRr))[0]), 4)],
        "rr_cal": [round(float(np.exp(ci.logRr.iloc[0])), 2)],
        "ci_cal": [f"{np.exp(ci.logLb95Rr.iloc[0]):.2f}-{np.exp(ci.logUb95Rr.iloc[0]):.2f}"],
        "p_cal": [round(float(ec.calibrateP(null, logRr, seLogRr)[0]), 4)],
        "ease": [round(float(ec.computeExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError(null)), 3)],
    })

calibrated_report(null, positive.logRr.iloc[0], positive.seLogRr.iloc[0],
                  positive.drugName.iloc[0])
```
